==Problem 16==

A circle has been divided into <imath>6</imath> sectors of different sizes. Then <imath>2</imath> of the sectors are painted red, <imath>2</imath> painted green, and <imath>2</imath> painted blue so that no two neighboring sectors are painted the same color. One such coloring is shown below.

<asy>
unitsize(1.7cm);
pair O = (0, 0);
real R = 2;

pair A = (R, 0);
pair B = (0.5*R, 0.866*R);
pair C = (0, R);
pair D = (-R, 0);
pair E = (-0.954*R, -0.3*R);
pair F = (-0.22*R, -0.975*R);

path sector1 = O -- A .. arc(O,A,B) -- cycle;
path sector2 = O -- B .. arc(O,B,C) -- cycle;
path sector3 = O -- C .. arc(O,C,D) -- cycle;
path sector4 = O -- D .. arc(O,D,E) -- cycle;
path sector5 = O -- E .. arc(O,E,F) -- cycle;
path sector6 = O -- F .. arc(O,F,A) -- cycle;

pen r = rgb(255, 120, 120); 
pen g = rgb(120, 255, 120); 
pen b = rgb(120, 120, 255);
filldraw(sector1, g);
filldraw(sector2, r);
filldraw(sector3, b);
filldraw(sector4, r);
filldraw(sector5, g);
filldraw(sector6, b);

draw(circle(O, R));

defaultpen(fontsize(12pt));
label("green", (0.57*R, 0.32*R));
label("red", (0.16*R, 0.63*R));
label("blue", (-0.45*R, 0.45*R));
label("red", (-0.69*R, -0.1*R));
label("green", (-0.45*R, -0.5*R));
label("blue", (0.39*R, -0.49*R));
</asy>

How many different colorings are possible?


<imath>\textbf{(A)}~12\qquad\textbf{(B)}~16\qquad\textbf{(C)}~18\qquad\textbf{(D)}~24\qquad\textbf{(E)}~28</imath>

==Solution 1==

Consider the topmost sector of any given circle. Put a "marker" on it. Now, reflect the diagram and rotate it until the marker is in the same place as it was last time. What we have just constructed are two circles with different colorings, except that the unique sectors formed are the exact same. Thus, for any given circular diagram, another diagram exists that is the exact same as the prior one.

The number of such colorings that exist given an arbitrary circular diagram is <imath>2^4 \cdot 3 = 48</imath>. In all of these possible colorings, exactly two are in a bijection (correspondence, basically two are the exact same type of sector for any diagram are overcounted). Thus we divide the count by two, yielding the answer <imath>\boxed{24}</imath>.

Essentially, this is what my solution 2 was trying to imply, except more in a formal definition. I hope now one can see the intuition.

~Pinotation

If this did not make much sense, please check solution 3, which I believe I made to be beginner friendly.

==Solution 2==

Create an arbitrary six slice circular diagram. The first slice has 3 options, and the second has 2, third has 2, fourth has 2, fifth has 2, and the sixth has only 1 color to be chosen.

Understand that if \( \mathbb{X} \) is the set containing all possible cases of the circle, then \( \mathbb{X} \) has a correlation to another set, call it \( \mathbb{K} \), which contains all the colors. This can be quite easily sought as a rotation of one element in \( \mathbb{X} \) that accurately maps to another element in \( \mathbb{X} \) is considered the same.

In simpler terms, to account for overlapping cases in \( \mathbb{X} \), one must divide by 2 (as two colorings that are rotated are considered different, and we don't want that as it defeats the purpose of "unique").

Then, multiplying out we have \( 3 \times 2^4 = 48 \). Dividing by 2 to account for overlap in \( \mathbb{X} \), we get \( 48/2 \) or
<imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 24}</imath>

~Pinotation

==Solution 3 ==

We can have <imath>3 \cdot 3 \cdot 2 \cdot 2 = 36</imath> unique colorings. Obviously, not all of these work. Particularly, we can have colorings in which 1, 2, or 3 colorings are adjacent. In case 1, we have 3 ways to choose that, and 2 ways to arrange the alternating colors. That is 6 ways total. In case 2, we have the case degenerates to case 3, in which we have again, 6 ways to determine as such. The answer is <imath>36 - 6 -6 = \boxed{24}</imath>.

~Pinotation

Notice we do not CHOOSE the colorings as the sectors are distinguishable.

==Solution 4==
 
Model the circle as the <imath>6</imath>-cycle \(C_6\) with labeled positions \(1,2,3,4,5,6\) in circular order. We count proper colorings using \(R,G,B\), each appearing exactly twice.

There are two structural possibilities for how the two copies of each color are placed:


{Case 1: All three colors occupy opposite positions.}


Opposite positions in \(C_6\) are the three pairs \((1,4), (2,5), (3,6)\). If each color occupies one opposite pair, then the colors must alternate around the circle, yielding a pattern of the form
{<imath>A,B,C,A,B,C</imath>}

for some ordering \((A,B,C)\) of \((R,G,B)\). The number of such colorings is <imath>3!</imath> = <imath>6</imath>


{Case 2: Exactly one color occupies opposite positions.}


Choose the color that is opposite: \(3\) choices. Choose which opposite pair it occupies: \(3\) choices one of \((1,4), (2,5), (3,6)\)), for a total of \(3\cdot 3 = 9\) placements.

Removing those two opposite positions leaves two disjoint adjacent pairs among the remaining four positions. For example, if the opposite color is at \((1,4)\), the remaining positions \(\{2,3,5,6\}\) form the two adjacent pairs \((2,3)\) and \((5,6)\). The other two colors must each appear twice, and no adjacent positions may match; therefore each pair must be colored with different colors, and to achieve two copies of each color overall, the two pairs must be complementary:

<imath>(2,3)</imath> is <imath>(G,B)</imath> or <imath>(B,G)</imath>, and then <imath>(5,6)</imath> in the opposite ordering.

This gives \(2\) valid assignments for the four positions per fixed opposite placement.

Hence, this case contributes
\(9\cdot 2 = 18\)

Summing the <imath>2</imath> cases

<imath>6</imath> + <imath>18</imath> = <imath>24</imath>

<imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 24}</imath>.

~NumberNinja1234

~Extremely minor edit by Boywithnuke

==Solution 5==

We can also case differently.

Let us call the sectors <imath>1</imath>, <imath>2</imath>, <imath>3</imath>, <imath>4</imath>, <imath>5</imath>, and <imath>6</imath> going clockwise around the circle. We, without loss of generality, assume <imath>1</imath> to be colored <imath>R</imath>. Additionally, without loss of generality, assume <imath>2</imath> to be colored <imath>B</imath>. We will nullify these assumptions by multiplying by a factor of <imath>6</imath> at the end.

We case on the color of sector <imath>6</imath>.

===Case 1: Sector <imath>6</imath> is colored <imath>B</imath>===

Each color is used two times, so we have one <imath>R</imath> and two <imath>G</imath>s left to distribute between <imath>3</imath>, <imath>4</imath>, and <imath>5</imath>. Obviously, the <imath>G</imath>s cannot be adjacent and thus the only possible coloring is <imath>(3, 4, 5) = (G, R, G)</imath>.

There is <imath>1</imath> solution for this case.

===Case 2: Sector <imath>6</imath> is colored <imath>G</imath>===

In this case, we have we have one <imath>R</imath>, one <imath>B</imath>, and one <imath>G</imath> left to distribute between <imath>3</imath>, <imath>4</imath>, and <imath>5</imath>. Since <imath>3</imath>, <imath>4</imath>, and <imath>5</imath>, are all distinct colors, the only restrictions on this case are that <imath>3</imath> cannot be colored <imath>B</imath> and <imath>5</imath> cannot be colored <imath>G</imath>.

Quick casework shows that if <imath>3</imath> is colored <imath>R</imath>, there are one solution <imath>(3, 4, 5) = (R, G, B)</imath> and if <imath>3</imath> is colored <imath>G</imath> then there are two solutions <imath>(3, 4, 5) = (G, R, B)</imath> and <imath>(3, 4, 5) = (G, B, R)</imath>.

There are <imath>3</imath> solutions for this case.



Thus, the total number of solutions is: <cmath>6 \cdot (1 + 3) = \boxed{\textbf{(D) } 24}</cmath>

~megaboy6679

==Solution 6==
We can also have the following two cases:
===Case 1: The three colors on the top semicircle are all different===
Then, three are 6 different ways to rearrange the top. For the bottom, the leftmost one has one restriction and the rightmost one has one restriction. Let's say the leftmost cannot be red and the rightmost cannot be green WLOG. Then, we can have the cases (from left to right): {green, blue, red}, {green, red, blue}, and {blue, green, red}. So, there are 3 different ways to rearrange the bottom. So, ,for case one, there are <imath>6\times3=18</imath> different ways to rearrange.

===Case 2: The three colors on the top has one pair of the same colors===
Then, there are 3 ways to choose the same color and then 2 ways to choose the color that is only put in once. After choosing all of that, the bottom then will be fixed (try it yourself if you think it is not). So, case 2 has <imath>3\times2=6</imath> ways to rearrange.

After combining the 2 cases, we get <imath>18+6=24</imath> cases, so our answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 24}</imath>.

~Yuhao2012

==Solution 7 (simplest and easiest)==
Let's assume that the colors do not matter, so let's just start with Red in the very top sector. 
The fact that the sectors are distinct in size does not matter at all, so just ignore that. 
If Red is in the top sector, then we have 3 cases:

Case 1: Red is also in the 3rd sector (going clockwise from the top one)
Thus, this is only one case because there are already 2 that are together, so the colors of those 2 must be distinct. 

Case 2: Red is also in the sector directly opposite. 
There are 2 cases for this; we can have all the colors being opposite, or we can have a case where everything is symmetric. 

Case 3: Red is also in the 5th sector
This is basically congruent (symmetric) to the first case, so we also only have 1 case. 

Adding all these up, we have <imath>1+2+1=4</imath> cases in total.

However, we did not consider color yet. Because there are 3 colors, they can be permuted <imath>3!=6</imath> ways.  

Therefore, <imath>6\times4=24</imath>, so our answer is <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 24}</imath>.

~notvalid

==Solution 8==
We want to find the number of cases where we can arrange the colors <imath>A</imath>, <imath>B</imath>, and <imath>C</imath>, fixing <imath>A</imath> at the top, and assuming <imath>B</imath> and <imath>C</imath> are symmetrical, so switching all instances of them wouldn't count. Starting from the top-left sector and moving clockwise, we could do <imath>ABCACB</imath>, which is what was on the example, <imath>ABCABC</imath>, <imath>ABACBC</imath>, or <imath>ABCBAC</imath>, so there are four cases. Then, we can just multiply the number of cases by <imath>6</imath>, because that's how many ways we can rearrange <imath>A</imath>, <imath>B</imath>, and <imath>C</imath>, to get <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 24}</imath>.
Additionally, we could cheese by noting that the answer is just the number of cases times <imath>6</imath>, so the answer choice must be a multiple of <imath>6</imath>, so it's either <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(C) } 18}</imath> or <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 24}</imath>, in which case it's possible to just guess the fifty-fifty.

~vaishnav

==Solution 9==

Consider only half the circle. We only need to worry about three distinct colors on the upper half of the circle. There are <imath>3! = 6</imath> ways to arrange the three colors on the semicircle and again <imath>3! = 6</imath> ways to arrange the other same three colors on the bottom semicircle. In total, we have <imath>6 \cdot 6 = 36</imath> total ways. Now, we note that when we put the two semicircles together to create a full circle, we're only concerned that the end two sectors of each semicircle don't match(since each semicircle is arranged with three distinct colors already). Out of the <imath>6</imath> permutations(for instance <imath>B, R, G</imath> or <imath>B, G, R</imath> and so on), we need to take one permutation and figure out how many permutations don't work. In other words, if we have the permutation <imath>B, R, G</imath> how many permutations other than this one either start with a <imath>B</imath> or end with a <imath>G</imath>? Doing the very easy casework, we see that in this particular case only <imath>B, G, R</imath> and <imath>R, B, G</imath> don't work. Therefore, for every permutation, there are <imath>2</imath> permutations that don't work. Since we have <imath>6</imath> permutations, our final answer is

<imath>36 - 6 \cdot 2 = \boxed{24}</imath>

~ilikemath247365

==Solution 10(force)==
Say that we make a hexagon, with each vertices being a color on its own. We first denote the top vertices with a random color, say <imath>B</imath>. After the top vertex is decided, only the bottom 3 vertices are clear for <imath>B</imath>. The first case, where <imath>B</imath> is at the bottom right vertex, has 2 combinations possible. The second case, where <imath>B</imath> is at the bottom vertex, has 4 combinations. The third case, where <imath>B</imath> is at the bottom left vertex, has the mirrored value of 2 along with the first case. Multiplying all combinations by 3 gives us 24.

<imath>3 \cdot 8 = 24</imath>

~Alomonde~

==Solution 11 (word permutations)==
Let <imath>R</imath> denote a red segment, <imath>G</imath> denote a green segment, and <imath>B</imath> denote a blue segment. Let x represent a blank in this solution

Case 1: <imath>R x R x x x</imath>
There are 2 possibilities: <imath>RGRBGB</imath> and <imath>RBRGBG</imath>

Case 2: <imath>R x x R x x</imath>
There are 4 possibilities: <imath>RBGRBG</imath>, <imath>RGBRGB</imath>, <imath>RBGRGB</imath>, and <imath>RGBRBG</imath>.

Case 3: <imath>R x x x R x</imath>
Similar to case 1, there are 2 possibilities

A total of 8 possibilities have been counted, and since the R in those spots can also either be G or B, we multiply by 3 to get <imath>\boxed{\textbf{(D) } 24}</imath>

(Note: <imath>R x x x x R</imath> is not a possibility since we're dealing with a wheel! An easy pitfall to be careful of)

~iambaconiamgod~
